title: You Got a Lump Sum: What to Do First So It Doesn't Disappear
description: A bonus, a tax refund, an inheritance or a payout. Park it for 30 days, check what's really yours, follow a simple order, and say no to the pitches.

data.text: It rarely feels like a problem

A bonus at work. A tax refund. An inheritance. An insurance payout. A settlement. Money from selling something. A gift. The first feeling is luck. Three months later, many people look at their account and wonder where it went.
Windfalls disappear for ordinary reasons: spending feels free, everyone suddenly has a need, there's no plan, and strong emotions like excitement or grief push you to act fast.
Step 1: Pause. Park it for 30 days

Put the money in a separate, safe savings account and make no big decisions for 30 days. This gives emotions time to settle, a plan time to form, and gives you a reason to say “not yet” to everyone who has a suggestion.

data.title: The 30-day rule is your shield
data.text: “I've made a plan for this money, and I'm not deciding anything for 30 days.” It works on family, friends, salespeople and scammers.
There's one exception: if something urgent is due, such as overdue rent, power about to be cut or a repair you can't live without, handle that first.
Step 2: Check what you actually have

Some lump sums are taxed, and some come with costs. A bonus may already have had tax taken out. An inheritance may have bills or costs attached. A settlement may have fees. Rules differ by country, so find out what is really yours, and set aside any tax you may owe. For a large amount, get advice from a qualified local professional before big moves.
Step 3: Use a simple order
1. Anything urgent: overdue rent, utilities, an essential repair.
2. A starter emergency fund: at least one month of must-pay costs.
3. High-interest debt, like credit cards.
4. One goal that improves your life: training, equipment, moving costs.
5. A planned fun slice, around 5% to 10%.
6. The rest: longer-term savings, investing or insurance.

data.title: A $5,000 bonus
data.text: Elena's bonus is $5,000. Her must-pay costs are $1,500 a month. Her plan: $500 for fun (10%), $1,500 for a starter emergency fund (one month of costs), $2,500 to pay off a credit card at 24% interest, and $500 for a course. That adds up to $500 + $1,500 + $2,500 + $500 = $5,000.

data.title: What paying off the card is worth
data.text: $2,500 at 24% a year costs $2,500 × 0.24 = $600 in interest a year. Paying it off saves that $600 every year the debt would have stayed.
Why the fun slice matters
Plans with no fun tend to fail. A small, planned amount you're allowed to enjoy makes it much easier to leave the rest alone. Decide it in advance, spend it, and enjoy it guilt-free.
Step 4: Say no to the pitches

Lump sums attract attention. Relatives ask for help. A friend has a business idea. Someone offers a “guaranteed” return. A stranger offers to “recover” or “release” your money for a fee. Say: “I've made a plan, and I'm not deciding anything for 30 days.”

data.title: The cousin with a deal
data.text: Tomás gets $8,000 from an inheritance. A cousin says, “Put $5,000 into my business and it will double in three months.” Doubling in three months is a red flag. Tomás says, “I'm not deciding anything for 30 days.” He uses that time to check the claims, and to see whether he still wants to.
If the money came with grief
Money from a death or loss can feel heavy. There's no rush. Handle essentials, park the rest, and take your time. Avoid decisions you can't undo until you're ready.
If it comes every year
A tax refund or yearly bonus is predictable, so decide in advance. A pre-decided split removes the temptation to improvise.

data.title: A split for a $1,200 refund
data.text: Decide the split ahead: 60% to savings or debt, 30% to a goal, 10% for fun. On $1,200 that's $1,200 × 0.60 = $720, $1,200 × 0.30 = $360 and $1,200 × 0.10 = $120. Together, $720 + $360 + $120 = $1,200.

data.title: Make your split
data.text: Think of money you might receive this year. Write the split you'd choose now: urgent, emergency fund, debt, goal, fun, the rest.

data.title: What to remember
points: Park it in a separate account for 30 days before big decisions.
Check taxes and costs so you know what you really have.
A simple order: urgent, emergency fund, high-interest debt, one goal, a planned fun slice, the rest.
“Doubling in three months” and “guaranteed” are red flags.
Use the 30-day rule to say no to every pitch.
Predictable windfalls can have a split decided in advance.

data.text: The one thing to remember

data.title: Make a plan before the money feels spent
data.text: Thirty days of patience can decide whether a windfall changes your life or just your month.

quiz.question: You receive a lump sum. What is a good first move?
options: Spend some right away to enjoy it
Park it in a separate savings account and avoid big decisions for 30 days
Lend it to the first person who asks
quiz.explanation: A pause gives emotions time to settle and lets a plan form.

quiz.question: Elena sets aside 10% of her $5,000 bonus for fun. How much is that?
Elena pays off $2,500 of credit card debt at 24% a year. About how much interest does she save in a year?
Some lump sums may be taxed or come with costs, so you should check before spending all of it.
quiz.explanation: Taxes, fees or debts can reduce what is truly yours. Check first.

quiz.question: Which usually comes before investing?
options: Urgent bills and a starter emergency fund
quiz.explanation: Cover urgent needs and build a small safety net before taking risks with the rest.

quiz.question: A relative says, “Put $5,000 in my business and it will double in three months.” What is the best response?
options: Borrow more so you can invest more
Say yes quickly before the chance disappears
quiz.explanation: Fast doubling and pressure to hurry are red flags. A 30-day pause lets you check the facts.

quiz.question: You decide to split a $1,200 tax refund 60% / 30% / 10%. How much is the 60% share?
Why is a planned fun slice helpful?
options: It makes it easier to stick to the rest of the plan
It increases the interest on your debt
It removes the need for an emergency fund
quiz.explanation: A small, planned treat makes the rest of the plan easier to follow.
